column9: stem
column14: option_a
column15: option_b
column16: option_c
column17: option_d
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: In a water molecule, what type of bond holds each hydrogen atom to the oxygen atom?
column14: Covalent bond
column15: Hydrogen bond
column16: Ionic bond
column17: Metallic bond
column28: Inside one water molecule, the oxygen atom and each hydrogen atom share a pair of electrons, and sharing electrons is a covalent bond. The common mistake is picking hydrogen bond: hydrogen bonds are the weaker attractions BETWEEN separate water molecules, not the bonds inside one.
column29: Hydrogen bonds connect one water molecule to another. This question is about the bonds inside a single molecule.

column9: In a water molecule, both hydrogen atoms are bonded to a single ___ atom, which sits at the bend of the molecule.
column28: Water is H₂O: one oxygen atom in the middle with two hydrogen atoms attached to it, which gives the molecule a bent (V) shape. A common mistake is thinking the two hydrogens bond to each other; each hydrogen bonds only to the oxygen.
column29: Look at the formula H₂O. Which element is there only one of?

column9: A water molecule is neutral overall, yet it is called polar. How can both be true?
column14: Its oxygen atom is an ion with a full negative charge, while its hydrogens have full positive charges that cancel it out
column15: Its charges balance overall, but oxygen pulls the shared electrons closer, so its ends are slightly charged
column16: It is neutral only when it is frozen into ice, and it becomes polar once it melts
column17: It gains an extra electron whenever it is a liquid
column28: Neutral describes the whole molecule: its positive and negative charges balance out. Polar describes how that charge is spread out. Oxygen pulls the shared electrons closer, so the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen ends are slightly positive. The common mistake is thinking polar means water has full charges like an ion; it only has partial charges.
column29: Neutral is about the total charge. Polar is about where the charge sits.

column9: In a diagram of a water molecule, the symbol δ− (delta minus) is written next to the oxygen atom. What does δ− mean?
column14: Oxygen has a full −1 charge, like a chloride ion
column15: Oxygen has lost one of its electrons to hydrogen
column16: Oxygen has a slight (partial) negative charge
column17: Oxygen has an extra neutron in its nucleus
column28: The Greek letter δ (delta) means partial, so δ− is a slight negative charge, not a full one. It shows that the shared electrons spend more time near oxygen. A common mistake is reading δ− as a full −1 charge, which would make water an ion.
column29: The δ symbol is used for charges that are smaller than a full charge.

column9: Most of water's life-supporting properties trace back to one feature of the water molecule. Which feature is it?
column14: Its clear color, which lets sunlight pass through it
column15: Its lack of taste and smell, which makes it safe to drink
column16: Its large size compared with most other molecules
column17: Its polarity (uneven charge across the molecule)
column28: Water's polarity lets each molecule attract its neighbors and other charged or polar substances. That one feature leads to cohesion, adhesion, high specific heat, floating ice, and water's dissolving power. Color and taste don't explain any of these, and water is actually a small molecule.
column29: Pick the feature that would let water molecules attract each other.

column9: Which statements describe a single water molecule? Choose all that apply.
column14: It is neutral overall
column15: Its oxygen end is slightly negative and its hydrogen ends are slightly positive
column16: Its two hydrogen atoms are bonded to each other
column17: It is an ion with a full charge
column18: It has a bent shape, not a straight line
column28: Water is bent, neutral overall, and polar: slightly negative at the oxygen end and slightly positive at the hydrogen ends. The hydrogens bond only to the oxygen, not to each other. Water has partial charges, not full charges, so it is not an ion.
column29: Water is polar but not an ion. Keep that in mind for each choice.

column9: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is a straight molecule with an oxygen on each side of the carbon, and it is nonpolar. Water (H₂O) is bent, with both hydrogens on the same side. Why does water's bent shape matter?
column14: Both hydrogens sit on one side, so that side is slightly positive and the oxygen side slightly negative
column15: The bent shape makes each water molecule heavier than a CO₂ molecule, so water molecules pull harder on each other
column16: A bent shape means water has no covalent bonds, only weak attractions between its atoms
column17: The bent shape lets water conduct electricity like a metal does
column28: In a straight molecule like CO₂, the pulls on the electrons cancel out. In bent water, the slightly positive hydrogens are both on one side, so the molecule has a positive side and a negative side: it is polar. A common mistake is thinking polarity depends only on which atoms are present; shape matters too. Water is actually lighter than CO₂.
column29: Picture where the slightly positive hydrogens sit. Are they spread evenly around the molecule?

column9: A plastic comb rubbed on hair picks up a negative charge. When the comb is held near a thin stream of tap water, the stream bends toward the comb. What is the best explanation?
column14: The negative comb attracts the slightly negative oxygen ends of the water molecules, so the whole stream is pulled over
column15: Water molecules turn their slightly positive hydrogen ends toward the comb, so the stream is pulled toward it
column16: The comb heats the water, which makes the stream bend
column17: Water is nonpolar, so the comb's charge pulls evenly on every part of the stream
column28: Opposite charges attract. Because water is polar, the molecules turn so their slightly positive hydrogen ends face the negative comb, and the stream bends toward it. The common mistake is choosing oxygen: the oxygen end is slightly negative, so a negative comb would push it away, not pull it.
column29: Which end of a water molecule has the opposite charge from the comb?

column9: Methane (CH₄) is a nonpolar molecule about the same size and mass as water. Methane boils at −162 °C, but water boils at 100 °C. Which explanation fits best?
column14: Methane has more atoms in each molecule, so its molecules fly apart into a gas more easily
column15: Water molecules are much heavier than methane molecules, so it takes far more heat to get them moving fast enough to boil
column16: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, and breaking them to make a gas takes a lot of energy
column17: Water has ionic bonds between its molecules that must break before it can boil
column28: Methane and water are about the same size, so size and mass can't explain a 262-degree difference. The difference is hydrogen bonding: water molecules cling to one another, so it takes much more energy to separate them into a gas. Methane is nonpolar and can't form hydrogen bonds. Water has no ionic bonds.
column29: The molecules are about the same size, so look for a difference in how strongly the molecules attract each other.

column9: A student says, "Water is polar because it has more hydrogen atoms than oxygen atoms." Which response best corrects the student?
column14: The student is right: hydrogen atoms carry positive charge, so any molecule with more hydrogens than other atoms will end up polar
column15: Water is actually nonpolar, because its positive and negative charges cancel out to zero
column16: Water is polar because it is a liquid at room temperature, and liquids are polar while gases are not
column17: Counting atoms doesn't decide it. Oxygen pulls the shared electrons harder and the molecule is bent, so its charge is uneven
column28: Polarity comes from uneven sharing of electrons plus the molecule's shape. Methane (CH₄) has four hydrogens for every carbon and is still nonpolar, so the student's rule fails. Being a liquid has nothing to do with being polar.
column29: Polarity depends on how the electrons are shared and on the molecule's shape.

column9: In a molecule model kit, red balls are oxygen atoms and white balls are hydrogen atoms. A student builds two water molecules and wants to show a hydrogen bond between them with a dashed line. Where should the dashed line go?
column14: From a white ball on one molecule to the red ball on the other
column15: From a red ball on one molecule to the red ball on the other
column16: From a white ball on one molecule to a white ball on the other
column17: Between the red ball and a white ball inside the same molecule
column28: A hydrogen bond is the attraction between a slightly positive hydrogen on one molecule and the slightly negative oxygen on a different molecule, so it runs from white to red across the two molecules. Oxygen-to-oxygen or hydrogen-to-hydrogen would be like charges, which repel. A line inside one molecule would be a covalent bond, not a hydrogen bond.
column29: Opposite partial charges attract. Which color has which partial charge?

column9: In a glass of liquid water, what happens to the hydrogen bonds between the molecules?
column14: They never break once they form, which is why water holds together
column15: They constantly break and re-form as the molecules move around
column16: They exist only in ice, not in liquid water
column17: They slowly turn into covalent bonds
column28: Liquid water molecules are always moving, so hydrogen bonds are constantly breaking and forming again with new neighbors. That is why water can flow but still holds together. Hydrogen bonds exist in liquid water too; in ice they just lock into place. They never become covalent bonds.
column29: Liquid water flows. What would have to happen to the attractions between molecules for that to be possible?

column9: When sugar is stirred into water, water molecules surround each sugar molecule and pull it away from the crystal. What is this process called?
column14: Melting
column15: Evaporating
column16: Dissolving
column17: Freezing
column28: Water pulling sugar molecules away and spreading them through the liquid is dissolving. The common mistake is calling it melting; melting is a solid turning to liquid because of heat, and the sugar never becomes liquid sugar.
column29: The sugar is not getting hot. It is mixing into the water molecule by molecule.

column9: When an ice cube melts into liquid water, what happens at the level of the molecules?
column14: The covalent bonds break, and water splits into hydrogen gas and oxygen gas
column15: The water molecules become nonpolar
column16: New covalent bonds form between neighboring molecules
column17: Some hydrogen bonds between the molecules break, but every molecule is still H₂O
column28: Melting is a physical change. Heat breaks some of the hydrogen bonds that held the molecules in the ice crystal, so the molecules can slide past each other. The covalent bonds inside each molecule stay whole, so it is still H₂O. Thinking melting breaks the molecule apart is the common mistake.
column29: Melted ice is still water. What must stay the same, and what must change?

column9: Each of a water molecule's two hydrogen atoms can form one hydrogen bond with a neighbor, and its oxygen atom can form two more. What is the greatest number of hydrogen bonds one water molecule can form at the same time?
column28: 2 bonds through the hydrogens + 2 bonds through the oxygen = 4. In ice, each molecule is locked into all 4, which holds the molecules in an open pattern. A common mistake is answering 2 by counting only the hydrogen atoms.
column29: Count the hydrogen side and the oxygen side separately, then combine them.

column9: Hydrogen bonds are weak compared with covalent bonds. Why do they still have such a big effect on water's properties?
column14: Huge numbers of them form among trillions of water molecules, so together their pull adds up
column15: They form only in ice, where they are strongest
column16: They turn water molecules into ions, which attract each other very strongly
column17: Each single hydrogen bond is actually stronger than an ionic bond, so just a few of them hold water together
column28: One hydrogen bond is weak, but a single drop of water has trillions of molecules, each bonded to its neighbors. Added together, those bonds hold water together strongly enough to cause surface tension, high specific heat, and floating ice. They are not stronger than ionic bonds, and they don't make ions.
column29: Think about one thread compared with a rope made of thousands of threads.

column9: Imagine that water molecules suddenly could not form hydrogen bonds with each other. Which changes would you predict? Choose all that apply.
column14: Each water molecule would lose one of its hydrogen atoms
column15: Salt crystals would become nonpolar
column16: Water would boil at a much lower temperature
column17: Water would climb less well up a thin glass tube
column18: Sweat would carry away less heat as it evaporates
column28: Hydrogen bonds are behind water's high boiling point, its strong cohesion (needed for capillary action), and the large amount of heat it takes to evaporate. Without them, all three would drop. The number of atoms in each molecule would not change, because covalent bonds set that. Salt is ionic no matter what water does.
column29: For each choice, ask: does this depend on water molecules pulling on each other?

column9: A paper clip placed gently on top of a cup of water rests on the surface instead of sinking. Which property of water makes this possible?
column14: High specific heat
column15: Surface tension
column16: Water's ability to dissolve metal
column17: The low density of ice
column28: At the surface, water molecules pull tightly on each other (cohesion), forming a stretchy skin called surface tension. A light object like a paper clip can rest on that skin even though steel is denser than water. Break the skin and the clip sinks. Specific heat is about temperature, not this.
column29: The paper clip is denser than water, so something at the very top of the water must be holding it up.

column9: You slowly add water to a glass until the water rises a little above the rim in a dome, without spilling. What holds the dome together?
column14: Adhesion between the water and the air above the glass
column15: Water's high specific heat
column16: Cohesion: water molecules pulling on one another
column17: Evaporation from the top
column28: Water molecules attract each other through hydrogen bonds (cohesion), so the top layer holds together and bulges up before it spills. Water is barely attracted to air, so adhesion to air is the common wrong pick.
column29: Which molecules are doing the holding: water and air, or water and water?

column9: Why are small raindrops nearly round as they fall?
column14: Air pushes evenly on every side of the falling drop and squeezes it into a ball
column15: Raindrops freeze into balls high in the clouds and stay round after they melt
column16: Gravity pulls equally on all sides of a raindrop, so it rounds out
column17: Water molecules pull inward on one another, and a sphere has the least surface
column28: Cohesion pulls every water molecule toward its neighbors, so the drop squeezes into the shape with the smallest surface: a sphere. That same inward pull at the surface is surface tension. Falling raindrops are liquid, not frozen balls, and gravity pulls them down, not inward from every side.
column29: Water molecules at the edge of the drop are pulled toward the water inside it.

column9: Surface tension on water is caused mainly by
column14: cohesion among the water molecules at the surface
column15: adhesion of water to the air molecules just above it
column16: water's high specific heat
column17: salt dissolved in the water
column28: Molecules at the surface are pulled by neighbors beside and below them but not by the air above, so they hold together tightly, like a stretched skin. That pull is cohesion. Air is not strongly attracted to water, so adhesion to air is the wrong pick.
column29: Which is water more attracted to: air, or other water molecules?

column9: In a lab, students count how many drops fit on a penny before the liquid spills over. Water holds far more drops than rubbing alcohol does. What explains this?
column14: Alcohol is denser than water
column15: Water molecules have stronger cohesion because of their hydrogen bonds
column16: Alcohol molecules are attracted to the copper penny more strongly than water is
column17: Water has a higher specific heat
column28: Water's many hydrogen bonds give it strong cohesion and high surface tension, so the drops can pile into a tall dome before it breaks. Alcohol molecules attract each other less, so the dome spills sooner. Specific heat is about temperature change, not how drops stack, and rubbing alcohol is actually less dense than water.
column29: The liquid that piles higher is the one whose molecules hold on to each other more strongly.

column9: Pepper flakes are sprinkled on a bowl of water and rest on the surface. When a soapy fingertip touches the center, the pepper rushes to the edges of the bowl. What did the soap do?
column14: It made the pepper flakes polar, so they were pushed away from the soapy finger
column15: It heated the water in the center, and the warmer water spread out toward the cooler edges of the bowl, carrying the pepper with it
column16: It weakened the pull between surface water molecules in the center, so the stronger pull near the edges dragged the pepper outward
column17: It made the water in the center denser, so it sank and pulled the surface outward
column28: Soap breaks up the attractions between water molecules at the surface, lowering surface tension in the center. The water near the edges still pulls strongly, so it tugs the surface, and the pepper riding on it, outward. The pepper isn't moving on its own, and the soap doesn't heat the water.
column29: If the skin gets weaker in one spot, which way does the stronger skin around it pull?

column9: Which of these are examples of cohesion (water attracted to water)? Choose all that apply.
column14: Raindrops cling to the outside of a glass window
column15: An ice cube floats in a drink
column16: A puddle cools slowly at night
column17: Two small water drops on a counter touch and merge into one bigger drop
column18: A drop of water holds together at the tip of a faucet before it falls
column28: Merging drops and a drop holding together at a faucet are both water molecules pulling on other water molecules. Raindrops clinging to a window are adhesion (water sticking to glass, a different substance). Floating ice is about density, and slow cooling is about specific heat.
column29: Look for examples where water is holding on to other water, not to something else.

column9: A fishing spider can rest on the surface of a pond, but a frog that hops onto the same spot breaks through. Which explanation is best?
column14: The frog is nonpolar, so water can't hold it up
column15: The spider has a higher specific heat than the frog
column16: Water has stronger cohesion under spiders than under frogs, because spiders give off a waxy chemical that pulls water together
column17: Surface tension can hold up only light objects with spread-out weight; the heavy frog breaks through the surface
column28: Surface tension is strong for its size but limited. A light spider with long, spread-out legs presses gently on the surface skin, so the skin holds. A frog is far heavier, so it breaks through. Water's cohesion is the same in both spots, and specific heat has nothing to do with floating.
column29: Surface tension is real but limited. What is very different about the spider and the frog?

column9: Mosquito larvae (wigglers) hang just under the surface of still water, breathing through a tiny tube that pokes up through the surface. Which property of water do they depend on to hang there?
column14: Surface tension
column15: Evaporative cooling
column16: High specific heat
column17: Water's ability to dissolve sugar
column28: The larva hangs from the surface skin made by cohesion among the top layer of water molecules. A film of oil spread on the water lowers surface tension, which is one way people control mosquitoes. Dissolving, evaporation, and specific heat don't hold anything up.
column29: The larva is hanging from the very top layer of the water.

column9: On a cool morning, tiny drops of dew cling to the silk threads of a spider web. The water sticking to the silk is an example of
column14: cohesion
column15: adhesion
column16: evaporation
column17: specific heat
column28: Adhesion is water sticking to a different substance, here spider silk. Cohesion is water sticking to water. The common mistake is mixing the two up; think of ad- as in adding on to something else.
column29: Is the water sticking to more water, or to something that is not water?

column9: Which example shows adhesion (water sticking to something that is not water)?
column14: A water drop pulls itself into a round bead on a waxed surface
column15: An ice cube floats in a glass
column16: Water droplets cling to your skin after a shower
column17: A lake warms slowly in spring
column28: Droplets clinging to skin are water attracted to a different substance: adhesion. A drop pulling itself into a bead is cohesion winning over adhesion. Floating ice is density, and slow warming is specific heat.
column29: Find the choice where water is holding on to something other than water.

column9: Water's ability to rise up through very narrow spaces, like the thin tubes inside a celery stalk, is called ___ action.
column28: Capillary action: water sticks to the walls of the narrow tube (adhesion) and pulls more water up behind it (cohesion). A common mix-up is calling it surface tension, which is the skin on top of water.
column29: Your tiniest blood vessels share this name.

column9: At a clinic, a nurse touches the tip of a very thin glass tube to a drop of blood from a finger prick. The blood moves up into the tube by itself, with no squeezing or suction. Blood is mostly water. What pulls it up the tube?
column14: The glass tube warms the blood so it rises
column15: Salts dissolved in the blood push it upward as they spread out into the empty tube
column16: Blood is less dense than the air in the tube
column17: The water sticks to the glass walls and pulls more water up behind it
column28: This is capillary action. Water in the blood is attracted to the glass (adhesion) and creeps up the walls, and because water molecules hold on to each other (cohesion), the rest of the blood follows. Blood is much denser than air, and warmth isn't what moves it.
column29: Think about two attractions: water to glass, and water to water.

column9: A white carnation is placed in a cup of water with blue food coloring. A day later, the petals have blue streaks. How did the dyed water get up the stem?
column14: Water stuck to the walls of thin tubes in the stem (adhesion) and pulled more water up behind it (cohesion)
column15: The flower absorbed blue light from the room
column16: Hydrogen bonds pushed the blue dye molecules out of the water and up into the petals, where they collected over time
column17: Ice crystals formed in the cold stem overnight and carried the dye up as they grew
column28: The stem is full of thin xylem tubes. Water clings to the tube walls (adhesion) and each water molecule tugs the next one along (cohesion), so the dyed water climbs, helped by water evaporating from the flower. Light color doesn't move water, and nothing froze.
column29: Think about two kinds of attraction working together inside very thin tubes.

column9: Water climbs higher in a very narrow glass tube than in a wide glass tube. Why?
column14: Narrow tubes stay colder, and cold water is pulled upward by the glass more strongly than warm water
column15: A narrow tube has more glass wall for each bit of water, so adhesion can lift the water higher
column16: Wide tubes have more surface tension, which presses down on the water and keeps it from climbing as high
column17: Water is denser in a wide tube
column28: Adhesion pulls on the water where it touches the glass. In a narrow tube there is a lot of glass wall compared with the small amount of water that has to be lifted, so the water rises higher. In a wide tube the same kind of pull has to lift much more water. Temperature and density are the same in both tubes.
column29: Compare how much water touches the glass with how much water has to be lifted.

column9: Mercury is a liquid metal whose atoms attract each other strongly but are barely attracted to glass. When a thin glass tube is dipped in mercury, the mercury inside the tube sits LOWER than the mercury outside. Water in the same kind of tube rises higher. What best explains the difference?
column14: Mercury is polar and water is not, so the glass pushes mercury down and pulls water up
column15: Mercury has a much higher specific heat than water, so it stays cooler and contracts down into the tube instead of climbing
column16: Water sticks to glass strongly, so it climbs; mercury holds on to itself much more than to glass, so it pulls away
column17: Water is denser than mercury
column28: Whether a liquid climbs a tube depends on its pull on the glass (adhesion) compared with its pull on itself (cohesion). Water is polar and sticks to glass, so it climbs. Mercury holds on to itself far more than to the glass, so it pulls down and away from the walls. Mercury is not polar, its specific heat is actually very low, and it is much denser than water.
column29: For each liquid, compare its pull on itself with its pull on the glass.

column9: Which of these depend on adhesion? Choose all that apply.
column14: A strip of filter paper dipped in water pulls water upward to separate ink colors
column15: Ice forms on the top of a pond
column16: A lake stays cool on a hot afternoon
column17: A dry sponge set in a puddle soaks water upward into its holes
column18: Water climbs the walls of the xylem tubes in a maple tree
column28: The sponge, the xylem, and the filter paper all have water climbing a surface that is not water, so adhesion is at work (with cohesion pulling more water along). Ice forming on top is about density, and a lake staying cool is about specific heat.
column29: Look for water touching and climbing something that is not water.

column9: Water's adhesion is strongest with which kind of surface?
column14: Nonpolar surfaces, like candle wax or a waxed car
column15: Only metal surfaces
column16: Every surface equally
column17: Polar or charged surfaces, like glass or cotton
column28: Water's slightly charged ends are attracted to other charges, so water sticks to polar surfaces like glass, paper, and cotton. Nonpolar surfaces like wax offer nothing for water to attract, so water beads up on them instead.
column29: Water's partly charged ends are attracted to other charges.

column9: Coast redwood trees move water more than 100 meters up from their roots to their leaves, with no pump. Which explanation is best supported by what you know about water?
column14: Evaporation from leaves pulls on the water in the xylem, and cohesion keeps that column of water from breaking
column15: Trees have a heart-like organ in their roots that squeezes water up through the trunk every few seconds, like a pump
column16: Water rises because it is less dense than air, so it floats upward through the trunk toward the leaves
column17: Water's high specific heat makes it expand as it warms in the sun, which pushes it up the trunk
column28: Water evaporating from the leaves tugs on the water below it. Because water molecules hold on to each other (cohesion), the whole column in the thin xylem tubes is pulled up like a chain, and adhesion to the tube walls keeps it from sliding back down. Trees have no pump, water is far denser than air, and warming doesn't push water up.
column29: Picture a long chain of water molecules holding hands inside a thin tube, with the top end being pulled.

column9: When you dip just the corner of a sugar cube into a cup of coffee, the coffee quickly spreads up through the whole cube. Which property of water is mainly at work?
column14: High specific heat, which lets the hot coffee rise through the cube
column15: Capillary action through the tiny spaces between the sugar grains
column16: The low density of ice
column17: Evaporative cooling, which draws coffee upward as it dries
column28: A sugar cube is full of tiny gaps between grains, like a bundle of narrow tubes. Coffee (mostly water) sticks to the grains (adhesion) and pulls more coffee along behind it (cohesion), so it climbs. That is capillary action. The other choices don't move liquid upward.
column29: The coffee is moving upward through very narrow spaces.

column9: Wet sand can be packed into a tall sandcastle tower, but dry sand just pours into a pile. Which explanation fits best?
column14: Water makes the sand grains denser and heavier, so they press together and can't slide apart
column15: Water's high specific heat cools the sand into a solid
column16: Water clings to the grains (adhesion) and to itself (cohesion), forming tiny bridges between the grains
column17: Water dissolves the outer layer of each sand grain into a sticky paste that glues neighboring grains together
column28: Thin films of water cling to each grain (adhesion), and the water between grains holds on to itself (cohesion), so the water acts like tiny bridges that hold the castle up. Sand doesn't dissolve in water, and temperature isn't what holds it together.
column29: Think about how water attaches to the grains and to the water between them.

column9: Each time you blink, a thin film of tears spreads across the surface of your eye and stays there. Tears are mostly water. What keeps the film stuck to your eye?
column14: Cohesion only, since tears are mostly water
column15: Evaporative cooling
column16: The high specific heat of tears, which keeps them warm
column17: Adhesion between the water and the surface of the eye
column28: The tear film is water sticking to a different surface, the eye, so it is adhesion. Cohesion keeps the film itself together, but it can't make the water stick to the eye. Specific heat and evaporation don't hold anything in place.
column29: The tears are sticking to something that is not water.

column9: On a sunny July afternoon at a Wisconsin lake beach, the sand is too hot to walk on barefoot, but the lake water still feels cool. What best explains this?
column14: Water has a higher specific heat than sand, so it takes more energy to warm up
column15: Water reflects all of the sunlight that hits it
column16: Sand has a higher specific heat than water, so it soaks up more heat from the sun
column17: Sand dissolves heat better than water
column28: Both got about the same sunlight, but water has a high specific heat: each gram needs a lot of energy to warm by one degree. Sand needs much less, so it heats up fast. The common mistake is thinking the thing that gets hotter has the higher specific heat; it's the opposite.
column29: The material that warms up slowly is the one that needs MORE energy per degree.

column9: How does water's high specific heat help the fish living in a large lake?
column14: It keeps the lake from ever freezing, even in the coldest part of a Wisconsin winter
column15: The lake's temperature changes slowly, so the fish avoid sudden temperature swings
column16: It lets the fish pull oxygen from the water without needing gills
column17: It makes the lake water taste fresher
column28: Because water needs a lot of energy to change temperature, a big lake warms and cools slowly. Fish get a steady environment instead of big daily swings. Lakes can still freeze on top in winter, and specific heat has nothing to do with taste or breathing.
column29: Think about what would happen to the fish if the water temperature jumped up and down every day.

column9: Specific heat is the amount of heat energy needed to
column14: melt 1 gram of ice
column15: turn 1 gram of liquid water completely into water vapor
column16: raise the temperature of 1 gram of a substance by 1 °C
column17: dissolve 1 gram of salt
column28: Specific heat measures how much energy it takes to warm 1 gram of a substance by 1 °C. Water's is high: 1 calorie per gram per °C. Melting and boiling take energy too, but those are changes of state, not specific heat.
column29: Specific heat is about changing temperature, not changing state.

column9: Water's specific heat is 1 calorie per gram per °C (1 cal/g·°C). How many calories are needed to raise the temperature of 50 g of water by 10 °C?
column28: Heat = mass × specific heat × temperature change = 50 g × 1 cal/g·°C × 10 °C = 500 calories. A common mistake is adding (50 + 10 = 60) instead of multiplying.
column29: Every gram needs 1 calorie for every degree. How many grams, and how many degrees?

column9: A beaker holds 200 g of water at 20 °C. A hot plate adds 3,000 calories of heat to the water. Water's specific heat is 1 cal/g·°C. If no heat is lost, what is the water's new temperature in °C?
column28: Temperature change = heat ÷ (mass × specific heat) = 3,000 ÷ (200 × 1) = 15 °C. The water started at 20 °C, so it ends at 20 + 15 = 35 °C. The common mistake is answering 15, which is only the change.
column29: First find how many degrees the water warmed, then use the starting temperature.

column9: Sand's specific heat is about 0.2 cal/g·°C, and water's is 1 cal/g·°C. The same amount of sunlight that warms 100 g of water by 2 °C would warm 100 g of sand by how many °C?
column28: The sunlight gave the water 100 g × 1 cal/g·°C × 2 °C = 200 calories. The same 200 calories warms 100 g of sand by 200 ÷ (100 × 0.2) = 10 °C, five times as much, because sand's specific heat is five times smaller. The common mistake is multiplying by 0.2 and getting 0.4 °C; a lower specific heat means a BIGGER temperature change.
column29: Find the calories of sunlight first, then ask how far those calories can warm the sand.

column9: Why does water have such a high specific heat?
column14: Water molecules are very heavy, so it takes a lot of energy to get them moving faster
column15: Water reflects heat instead of absorbing it
column16: Water has no attractions between its molecules
column17: Added heat first goes into breaking hydrogen bonds, so the molecules speed up slowly
column28: Temperature goes up only when molecules move faster. In water, a lot of the added energy first goes into breaking hydrogen bonds between molecules, so it takes more heat to raise the temperature. Water molecules are actually small and light, and water does absorb heat.
column29: Temperature rises only when molecules move faster. What has to be dealt with first in water?

column9: Cells are mostly water. Suppose cells were instead filled with a liquid that has a LOW specific heat. Which problem would organisms most likely face?
column14: Their cells' temperature would swing quickly, making it hard to keep conditions stable for cell reactions
column15: Their cells would dissolve, because liquids with low specific heat break down cell membranes
column16: Their cells would freeze solid on hot days, because low specific heat liquids lose all their heat at once
column17: Their cells could no longer hold any water
column28: A liquid with a low specific heat changes temperature with only a little heat. Cells would heat up and cool down fast, making homeostasis harder, and many cell reactions (run by enzymes) work well only in a narrow temperature range. Water's high specific heat buffers those swings.
column29: Low specific heat means it takes only a little energy to change the temperature.

column9: A camper wants to fill a bottle with a hot liquid to keep a sleeping bag warm all night. Which liquid would work best, and why?
column14: Rubbing alcohol, because it evaporates quickly
column15: Water, because its high specific heat lets it store a lot of heat and release it slowly
column16: A liquid with a low specific heat, because it heats up fastest and so it must hold the most heat
column17: Vegetable oil, because it is nonpolar
column28: The camper needs a liquid that holds a lot of heat and gives it up slowly. Water's high specific heat means each gram stores a lot of energy for each degree, and it cools slowly as it releases it. A low specific heat liquid heats fast but also cools fast, and evaporating alcohol would cool things down.
column29: You want the liquid that holds the most heat and gives it up slowly.

column9: Equal masses of water and ethanol (an alcohol) start at 20 °C and are heated on identical hot plates for 3 minutes. The water ends at 26 °C, and the ethanol ends at 30 °C. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: The ethanol's hot plate must have been hotter
column15: Ethanol has the higher specific heat, because it reached a higher temperature in the same time
column16: Water has the higher specific heat, because the same heat raised its temperature less
column17: Ethanol absorbed less heat than the water
column28: Both liquids got the same heat (identical hot plates, same time, same mass). Water warmed only 6 °C while ethanol warmed 10 °C, so water needs more energy per degree: it has the higher specific heat. The common mistake is thinking got hotter means holds more heat.
column29: Same heat, same mass. Which liquid resisted changing temperature?

column9: Equal masses of water and corn oil each absorb the same amount of heat. The water's temperature rises 10 °C, but the oil's rises 22 °C. Water's specific heat is 1.0 cal/g·°C. What is the oil's specific heat, in cal/g·°C? Round to two decimal places.
column28: Same heat and same mass, so specific heat × temperature change must match for both: 1.0 × 10 = c × 22, so c = 10 ÷ 22 ≈ 0.45 cal/g·°C. The oil warmed more, so its specific heat must be smaller than water's. Answering 2.2 (22 ÷ 10) is the common mistake; that ratio is upside down.
column29: The liquid that warmed more must have the smaller specific heat, so your answer should be less than 1.

column9: Two identical pots sit on identical burners. One holds 1 liter of water and the other holds 2 liters, both starting at the same temperature. Which pot reaches boiling first, and why?
column14: The 2-liter pot, because more water absorbs heat faster
column15: The 2-liter pot, because larger amounts of water have a lower specific heat
column16: They boil at the same time, because water's specific heat is the same no matter how much water there is
column17: The 1-liter pot, because less water needs less total heat to warm by the same amount
column28: Specific heat is per gram. Twice as much water needs twice as much heat to warm the same number of degrees, so with identical burners the 1-liter pot boils first. The trap is thinking same specific heat means same time: specific heat is the same per gram, but the total heat needed depends on the mass.
column29: Specific heat tells you the heat needed for EACH gram.

column9: Water's specific heat is 1 cal/g·°C. You have 400 calories of heat to add. How many grams of water can you warm by exactly 5 °C?
column28: Mass = heat ÷ (specific heat × temperature change) = 400 ÷ (1 × 5) = 80 g. Multiplying 400 × 5 = 2,000 is the common mistake.
column29: First figure out how many calories ONE gram needs for a 5 °C rise.

column9: Car engines are cooled by a liquid that is mostly water, pumped around the hot engine. Why is water a good choice?
column14: Its high specific heat lets it soak up a lot of heat while warming only a little
column15: It is nonpolar, so it slides through the engine's metal pipes without sticking to them
column16: Ice floats, so it won't clog the engine
column17: Its surface tension forms a tight skin over the hot metal that blocks heat from building up
column28: The coolant's job is to soak up heat from the engine and carry it away. Water's high specific heat lets it absorb a lot of energy while warming only a little. Water is polar, not nonpolar, and floating ice and surface tension don't remove heat.
column29: The coolant's job is to soak up heat.

column9: Equal masses of aluminum, copper, glass, and water are each warmed by 10 °C. Which one needs the most heat energy?
column14: Aluminum
column15: Water
column16: Glass
column17: Copper
column28: Water's specific heat (1 cal/g·°C) is much higher than that of metals or glass, so it needs the most energy to warm by the same amount. That's also why a metal spoon heats up faster than the soup it sits in.
column29: The substance with the highest specific heat needs the most energy per degree.

column9: You take a bite of a fresh, hot pizza. The crust feels warm, but the sauce burns your mouth. Both came out of the same oven. Which explanation fits best?
column14: The sauce is less dense than the crust, so heat moves through it faster and reaches your mouth first
column15: The crust is mostly water, so it cools instantly
column16: The sauce is mostly water, which has a high specific heat, so it holds more heat
column17: The sauce pulls heat out of your mouth
column28: The watery sauce stored much more heat in the oven than the dry crust did, because water has a high specific heat. When it touches your mouth, it releases that heat. The crust has little water, so it holds less heat and cools quickly.
column29: Which part of the pizza has the most water in it?

column9: Which of these show water's high specific heat? Choose all that apply.
column14: Salt disappears when stirred into water
column15: A big pot of soup stays hot long after the stove is turned off
column16: A swimming pool is still chilly in early June even after a week of warm days
column17: A drop of water beads up on a leaf
column18: An ice cube floats in a glass of tea
column28: The soup cooling slowly and the pool warming slowly both show that water resists changing temperature. A beading drop is cohesion, floating ice is density, and disappearing salt is water acting as a solvent.
column29: Look for water that is slow to change temperature.

column9: After sunset on a summer evening, the asphalt parking lot at a boat launch cools down quickly, but the lake next to it stays warm well into the night. Which property of the lake water explains this?
column14: The low density of ice
column15: Its surface tension, which traps heat under the surface like a lid
column16: Its ability to dissolve salts
column17: Its high specific heat, so it releases its stored heat slowly
column28: Water stores a lot of heat for each degree and gives it up slowly, so the lake cools slowly after dark. Asphalt has a much lower specific heat, so it loses its heat fast. Surface tension doesn't trap heat.
column29: Which property is about how fast something changes temperature?

column9: A student records temperatures at a pond. At 6 a.m., the air is 15 °C and the pond water is 21 °C. At 3 p.m., the air is 32 °C and the pond water is 23 °C. The student concludes, "The pond is warmer than the air all day." Which is the best evaluation?
column14: It's wrong: the air was warmer at 3 p.m. The data really show the pond's temperature stayed far steadier than the air's
column15: It's correct, because the pond was warmer than the air at 6 a.m., and water always stays warmer than air
column16: The data show that water has a low specific heat, because the pond's temperature kept rising all the way from early morning to afternoon
column17: The data show the pond absorbs heat from the air only at night, when the air is cooler than the water
column28: At 3 p.m. the air (32 °C) was warmer than the pond (23 °C), so the claim fails. The useful pattern is the size of the change: the air swung 17 °C but the pond only 2 °C, because water's high specific heat makes it slow to change temperature.
column29: Check the student's claim at both times, then compare how much each temperature changed.

column9: Water stays liquid from 0 °C to 100 °C at sea level. Why does this wide liquid range matter for life on Earth?
column14: It means water can never evaporate, so lakes and oceans never dry up and organisms always have water
column15: Most of Earth's surface stays in this range, so liquid water is there for organisms to use
column16: It means water can never freeze in nature
column17: It makes water a nonpolar solvent
column28: Most of Earth's surface stays between freezing and boiling most of the time, so water is usually a liquid where organisms live. Living things need liquid water to dissolve and move materials. Water does evaporate and freeze in nature; it just stays liquid across a wide range.
column29: Compare the range 0 °C to 100 °C with the temperatures where living things are found.

column9: On a hot day, a dog pants with its tongue hanging out. How does this cool the dog?
column14: It lets the dog swallow cold air, which cools its stomach and blood from the inside
column15: It makes the dog's blood more acidic
column16: Water evaporates from its tongue and mouth, and evaporating water carries heat away
column17: It adds hydrogen bonds to the dog's skin
column28: Dogs sweat very little through their skin, so they cool off by panting. Moving air speeds up evaporation from the wet tongue and mouth, and the evaporating water absorbs heat from the dog. The air itself isn't cold on a hot day.
column29: What is on the dog's tongue, and what happens to it in moving air?

column9: You climb out of a swimming pool on a warm, breezy day and suddenly feel chilly. Why?
column14: Pool water is always colder than the air
column15: The wind blows more water onto your skin from the pool, making you wetter and colder
column16: Your skin becomes nonpolar when it is wet
column17: Water on your skin evaporates, and evaporation takes heat energy away from your body
column28: Water needs a lot of energy to evaporate, and it takes that energy from your skin. The breeze speeds up evaporation, so you cool even faster. The pool water doesn't have to be colder than the air for this to happen.
column29: As your skin dries, where does the water go, and what does it take with it?

column9: Pigs have very few working sweat glands. On hot days they roll in mud. How does this help them stay cool?
column14: Water in the mud evaporates from their skin and carries heat away
column15: Mud makes the pigs denser, so they sink into cool ground
column16: Mud dissolves the extra heat in their skin
column17: Mud has a low specific heat, so it stays cold all afternoon in the sun
column28: The wet mud works like sweat: as its water evaporates, it absorbs heat from the pig's skin. Mud also dries slowly, so the cooling lasts longer. Heat doesn't dissolve, and a low specific heat would make mud warm up fast, not stay cold.
column29: Think about what sweat does for you, then look for the water in the mud.

column9: Put these steps in order to show how sweating cools you on a hot day.
column14: Water in the sweat absorbs heat from your skin and evaporates
column15: Your body temperature starts to rise
column16: Your skin cools down
column17: Sweat glands release water onto your skin
column28: First your body heats up, so sweat glands release water onto your skin. That water absorbs heat from your skin as it evaporates, and the loss of heat cools your skin. The common mistake is thinking the sweat itself is cold; the cooling comes from evaporation.
column29: Start with the problem (getting hot) and end with the result.

column9: A drop of rubbing alcohol and a drop of water are placed side by side on your arm. The alcohol evaporates first. What explains why it evaporates faster?
column14: Alcohol molecules are smaller and lighter than water molecules, so they float off into the air more easily
column15: Alcohol molecules attract each other less than water molecules do, so they escape into the air more easily
column16: Alcohol has a higher specific heat than water, so it absorbs body heat faster and boils off first
column17: Water is nonpolar, so it clings to skin
column28: To evaporate, a molecule has to break free of its neighbors. Water molecules are held by many hydrogen bonds, so water needs more energy to evaporate. Alcohol molecules attract each other less, so they escape sooner. Rubbing alcohol molecules are actually bigger and heavier than water molecules, so size can't explain it, and water is polar, not nonpolar.
column29: Evaporating means breaking free from neighbors. Compare how strongly each liquid's molecules hold on to one another.

column9: On a hot afternoon, a maple tree releases water vapor through tiny pores in its leaves. How does this help keep the leaves from overheating?
column14: It makes the leaves denser so they don't blow away in the wind
column15: It traps heat inside the leaf
column16: Evaporating water absorbs heat from the leaf, cooling it
column17: It breaks water's covalent bonds to release energy
column28: When water evaporates from a leaf, it takes heat energy with it, so the leaf cools, just like sweat cools your skin. Evaporation doesn't trap heat, and water molecules stay H₂O when they evaporate.
column29: Plants don't sweat, but they do something very similar.

column9: Elephants spray water on their backs on hot days. Water needs much more heat energy to evaporate than most liquids do. Why does this make water especially good for cooling?
column14: It means water evaporates almost instantly, so the elephant cools off the very moment the spray lands on its back
column15: It keeps the water frozen longer
column16: It makes the elephant's skin waterproof
column17: Each gram of water that evaporates carries away a lot of heat, so a little water removes a lot of heat
column28: The energy that evaporation needs comes from the elephant's skin. Because water needs so much energy per gram to evaporate, each gram carries away a lot of body heat. Needing more energy actually makes water evaporate more slowly, not instantly.
column29: If evaporating takes a lot of heat, where does that heat come from?

column9: On a humid day, sweat drips off your skin instead of evaporating, and you feel hotter than on a dry day at the same temperature. Which explanation is best?
column14: Less sweat evaporates, so less heat is carried away from your skin
column15: Humidity makes sweat nonpolar
column16: Dripping sweat removes more heat than evaporating sweat, so you sweat even more
column17: Humid air has a lower specific heat than dry air
column28: Sweat cools you only when it evaporates, because evaporation is what absorbs heat from your skin. Humid air already holds a lot of water vapor, so sweat evaporates slowly and drips off, carrying away very little heat. Humidity doesn't change whether water is polar.
column29: Which part of sweating actually removes the heat?

column9: Which of these are examples of evaporative cooling? Choose all that apply.
column14: Wet laundry hanging on a line feels cool to the touch as it dries
column15: A fan cools your face more when your face is damp
column16: An ice cube floats in a glass
column17: A big lake warms slowly in spring
column18: Water slowly seeps through the walls of an unglazed clay jug and evaporates, keeping the water inside cool
column28: In the clay jug, the drying laundry, and the damp face, water is evaporating from a surface and taking heat with it. A floating ice cube shows density, and a lake warming slowly shows specific heat.
column29: Look for water drying off a surface.

column9: Evaporating 1 g of sweat removes about 580 calories of heat from your skin. During a long run, your body needs to get rid of 58,000 calories of extra heat by sweating. How many grams of sweat must evaporate?
column28: 58,000 ÷ 580 = 100 g of sweat (about 100 mL). Multiplying 58,000 × 580 is the common mistake; you want how many 580-calorie portions fit into 58,000.
column29: Each gram removes 580 calories. How many grams does it take to reach 58,000?

column9: Ice cubes float at the top of a glass of lemonade. What does this tell you about ice?
column14: Ice is heavier than liquid water
column15: Ice is less dense than liquid water
column16: Ice is made of a different substance than water
column17: Ice is colder, and cold things always rise
column28: Something floats when it is less dense than the liquid it is in. Ice is less dense than liquid water, which is unusual: most solids are denser than their liquids and sink. Heavier is the common mistake; a big ice cube can weigh more than a little water and still float.
column29: Floating depends on density, not on weight or temperature.

column9: Suppose ice were denser than liquid water. What would most likely happen to a northern Wisconsin lake over a long, cold winter?
column14: The lake would never freeze at all, because sinking ice would melt in the warmer water at the bottom
column15: The lake would freeze only on top, just like it does now
column16: Ice would sink as it formed, so the lake could freeze solid from the bottom up, killing most fish
column17: The lake water would boil away
column28: If ice sank, each new layer would drop to the bottom and leave fresh water exposed to the cold air to freeze next. The lake could fill with ice from the bottom up. Because real ice floats, it forms a lid that keeps the water below liquid.
column29: If ice sank, where would each new layer of ice end up?

column9: An iceberg floats with about 90% of its volume underwater and only about 10% above the surface. What does this tell you?
column14: Ice is much denser than seawater
column15: Icebergs are hollow inside
column16: Ice and seawater have exactly the same density
column17: Ice is only slightly less dense than seawater
column28: A very light object, like a cork, floats high with most of it above the water. Because ice is only a little less dense than seawater, it floats low, with most of it hidden. If ice were denser than seawater, it would sink; if they were exactly equal, it wouldn't stick out at all.
column29: A very light object, like a cork, floats high. A barely lighter object floats low.

column9: Liquid water has a density of 1.00 g/mL, and ice has a density of 0.92 g/mL. If 92 g of liquid water freezes completely, what volume will the ice take up, in mL?
column28: Volume = mass ÷ density. The mass doesn't change when water freezes, so the ice takes up 92 g ÷ 0.92 g/mL = 100 mL. As a liquid, the same 92 g took up only 92 mL, so freezing made it expand. Multiplying 92 × 0.92 gives a smaller volume, which is backwards: ice takes up MORE space.
column29: Freezing doesn't change the mass. Use volume = mass ÷ density.

column9: Put these steps in order to explain why ice floats on liquid water.
column14: Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats.
column15: As water cools, its molecules slow down.
column16: The molecules end up farther apart than they are in liquid water.
column17: Hydrogen bonds lock each molecule to its neighbors in a fixed, open pattern.
column28: Cooling slows the molecules, so hydrogen bonds can lock them into a fixed, open, honeycomb-like pattern. That pattern holds the molecules farther apart than in the liquid, so ice is less dense and floats. A common mistake is thinking ice floats because of trapped air.
column29: Start with what happens as water gets colder, and end with floating.

column9: Potholes appear in Wisconsin roads in early spring after water seeps into small cracks and freezes and thaws over and over. Which property of water causes the damage?
column14: Water expands when it freezes, so the ice pushes the cracks wider
column15: Water's adhesion glues pieces of the road together
column16: Water dissolves the road surface instantly
column17: Water's high specific heat cools the road so much that the road surface shatters
column28: Water takes up more space as ice than as a liquid, because hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open pattern. Each freeze pushes the crack a little wider, and after many freeze-thaw cycles the road breaks apart. The same thing breaks rocks in nature.
column29: Compare the space water takes up as a liquid and as ice.

column9: After water dries on a shower door, it leaves white spots. Where did the white material come from?
column14: The glass melted slightly
column15: Minerals that were dissolved in the water were left behind when the water evaporated
column16: Soap scum that was never rinsed away, since soap is the only thing that leaves spots
column17: Oxygen that escaped from the water
column28: Tap water often carries dissolved minerals like calcium. Water is such a good solvent that it picks them up from rocks and soil. When the water evaporates, the minerals can't evaporate with it, so they stay behind as white spots.
column29: Before the water dried, something was dissolved in it.

column9: A student says, "Ice floats only because it has air bubbles trapped inside it." Which evidence would best show the student is wrong?
column14: Ice cubes from a home freezer are often cloudy with tiny bubbles
column15: Ice melts at 0 °C
column16: Perfectly clear ice with no bubbles still floats on water
column17: Ice cubes sink in rubbing alcohol
column28: If bubbles were the reason, bubble-free ice would sink. Clear ice still floats, so the real reason is the ice itself: hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open pattern that is less dense than liquid water. Cloudy ice and melting point don't test the claim, and sinking in alcohol only shows that alcohol is less dense than ice.
column29: To test whether it's the bubbles, take the bubbles away.

column9: Which of these would NOT dissolve when stirred into a glass of water?
column14: Granulated table sugar
column15: Table salt crystals
column16: Baking soda powder
column17: Candle wax shavings
column28: Sugar, salt, and baking soda dissolve because water's charged ends attract polar molecules and ions. Wax is nonpolar, so water molecules are more attracted to each other than to the wax, and the wax stays separate.
column29: Water dissolves things that are polar or charged. Which of these is nonpolar?

column9: Substances that are attracted to water and dissolve easily in it, like salt and sugar, are called ___, which means water-loving.
column28: Hydro- means water and -philic means loving, so hydrophilic substances are attracted to water. They are usually polar or charged. The opposite is hydrophobic (water-fearing), like oil and wax.
column29: It starts with hydro-, which means water.

column9: A greasy frying pan won't come clean with plain water, no matter how hard you rinse. Why?
column14: Grease is nonpolar, so water molecules are attracted to each other rather than to the grease
column15: Water is too cold to dissolve anything
column16: Grease is polar, so its partial charges push the water molecules away instead of attracting them
column17: Grease is denser than water, so the water can't reach it
column28: Water dissolves substances that are polar or charged, like itself. Grease is nonpolar, so water molecules stick to each other instead and roll right past it. That's why you need soap, which can grab both water and grease.
column29: Water dissolves things that are like it. Is grease like water?

column9: Ducks spread oil from a gland onto their feathers. When it rains, water beads up and rolls right off. What is happening?
column14: The water's adhesion to the oily feathers is stronger than its cohesion, so the water slides off
column15: The water's cohesion is stronger than its adhesion to the oily feathers, so it pulls into beads
column16: The oil heats the water so it evaporates
column17: The oil makes the water denser
column28: Oil is nonpolar, so water has almost nothing to stick to on the feathers (weak adhesion). Water's pull on itself (cohesion) wins, so it forms beads that roll off, keeping the duck dry and warm.
column29: Is oil something water likes to stick to? If not, what is water holding on to instead?

column9: When table salt dissolves, positive sodium ions (Na⁺) move into the water. Which part of nearby water molecules turns to face each Na⁺ ion?
column14: The hydrogen atoms
column15: Neither, because water has no charged ends
column16: The oxygen atom
column17: The hydrogens and the oxygen equally
column28: Opposite charges attract. Water's oxygen end is slightly negative, so it turns toward the positive Na⁺ ion. Picking hydrogen is the common mistake; the hydrogen ends are slightly positive and would be pushed away by Na⁺.
column29: Which end of a water molecule has the opposite charge from Na⁺?

column9: A student draws salt dissolving in water. In the drawing, water molecules surround a chloride ion (Cl⁻) with their oxygen atoms touching it. What is wrong with the drawing?
column14: Nothing is wrong; oxygen is the largest atom in water, so it always turns to face any ion that water surrounds
column15: The water molecules should be covalently bonded to the Cl⁻ ion, sharing electrons with it
column16: Chloride ions don't dissolve in water
column17: The water should face Cl⁻ with its slightly positive hydrogen ends, since opposite charges attract
column28: Cl⁻ is negative, and water's oxygen end is slightly negative too, so oxygen would be pushed away. The slightly positive hydrogen ends should point toward Cl⁻. Which end faces an ion depends on the ion's charge. The attraction is not a covalent bond.
column29: Check the charge on the ion, then find the end of water with the opposite charge.

column9: Why does a spoonful of table sugar dissolve easily in a glass of water?
column14: Sugar molecules are polar, so water molecules are attracted to them and pull them into the water
column15: Sugar reacts with water to form salt
column16: Water breaks the sugar molecules into separate carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms that spread out
column17: Sugar is nonpolar, just like water
column28: Like dissolves like. Sugar molecules have polar regions, so water molecules attach to them and carry them off into the water. The sugar molecules stay whole; they are just spread out. Water is polar, not nonpolar.
column29: Water dissolves substances that are like it. What is water like?

column9: Blood plasma is about 90% water. Why does this matter for carrying glucose, salts, and other nutrients around your body?
column14: Water makes the nutrients nonpolar so they move faster
column15: Water dissolves many polar and charged substances, so they can travel dissolved in the blood
column16: Water's density makes the nutrients sink to your feet
column17: Water breaks the nutrients down into single atoms, which are small enough to travel through blood vessels
column28: Because water is polar, it dissolves glucose, salts, and many other substances, so they can ride along in the blood to every cell. Dissolving doesn't change a molecule into a different one or break it into atoms.
column29: Think about what water does to salt and sugar.

column9: Solid iodine is made of nonpolar molecules. In which liquid would it dissolve best?
column14: Pure water, a polar liquid
column15: Salt water, which is full of ions
column16: Mineral oil, a nonpolar liquid
column17: Sugar water, which is very sweet
column28: Like dissolves like: nonpolar substances dissolve best in nonpolar liquids. Iodine dissolves only a little in water because water molecules would rather stick to each other. Adding salt or sugar doesn't make water nonpolar.
column29: Match the liquid to the substance: polar with polar, nonpolar with nonpolar.

column9: Which of these would you expect to dissolve well in water? Choose all that apply.
column14: Glucose, a polar sugar
column15: Vegetable oil
column16: Potassium chloride (KCl), an ionic compound
column17: Paraffin wax
column28: Water's charged ends pull apart ionic compounds like NaCl and KCl and attach to polar molecules like glucose, so all three dissolve. Oil, wax, and gasoline are nonpolar, so water molecules stick to each other instead and those substances stay separate.
column29: Water's charged ends attract things that are charged or polar.

column9: An unknown white powder dissolves easily in water but not at all in vegetable oil. What can you best infer about the powder?
column14: It is nonpolar
column15: It has a high specific heat
column16: It is a metal
column17: It is polar or made of ions
column28: Water dissolves polar and ionic substances, and oil dissolves nonpolar ones. Because the powder dissolves in water but not in oil, it is most likely polar or ionic, like sugar or salt. Specific heat doesn't tell you what will dissolve.
column29: Which kind of substance does water dissolve, and which kind does oil dissolve?

column9: Your kidneys remove wastes like urea from your blood and send them out of your body dissolved in urine, which is mostly water. Which property of water makes this possible?
column14: Water's polarity, which lets it dissolve many substances
column15: Water's surface tension, which holds the wastes together in drops
column16: Water's high specific heat, which keeps urine warm
column17: Ice being less dense than water
column28: Urea is a polar molecule, and water's polarity lets it dissolve urea and many other wastes so they can be carried out of the body. Specific heat, surface tension, and floating ice don't carry wastes.
column29: To be carried away in urine, the waste has to mix evenly into the water.

column9: Vitamin C dissolves in water, so extra vitamin C leaves your body in urine. Vitamin A dissolves in fat instead, so extra vitamin A is stored in body fat. Based on this, which is most likely true?
column14: Vitamin C is nonpolar, and vitamin A is polar
column15: Vitamin C is polar, and vitamin A is nonpolar
column16: Both vitamins are polar
column17: Both vitamins are nonpolar
column28: Like dissolves like. Vitamin C dissolves in water, so it must be polar. Vitamin A dissolves in fat, which is nonpolar like oil, so vitamin A must be nonpolar. That's why one washes out and the other is stored.
column29: Water dissolves polar substances; fat, like oil, dissolves nonpolar ones.

column9: Match each part of a glass of sweet tea to its role.
column14: Water :: Solvent
column15: Sugar :: Solute
column16: Sweet tea :: Solution
column28: Water does the dissolving, so it is the solvent. Sugar gets dissolved, so it is the solute. The even mixture of the two is the solution. A common mistake is swapping solute and solvent; the solvent is usually the substance there is the most of.
column29: The solvent is usually the substance there is the most of.

column9: A gardener sprinkles dry fertilizer pellets on a lawn. The grass can't use the nutrients until it rains. Why does rain help?
column14: Rain cools the pellets so the grass can absorb them
column15: Rain makes the pellets heavier and denser so they sink down through the grass into the soil
column16: The nutrients dissolve in the rainwater, which carries them into the soil to the roots
column17: Rain's surface tension pushes the pellets into the grass
column28: Roots take in nutrients only when they are dissolved in water. Rain dissolves the fertilizer and carries it down into the soil to the roots. Cooling, density, and surface tension don't make nutrients usable.
column29: Roots take in nutrients only when they are dissolved.

column9: A student stirs a spoonful of salt into a beaker of water, and the salt seems to disappear. What actually happened to the salt?
column14: It turned into water
column15: It evaporated into the air
column16: It sank to the bottom and became invisible because it is denser than water
column17: It broke apart into tiny ions that spread evenly through the water
column28: The salt dissolved: water molecules pulled the sodium and chloride ions apart and surrounded them, spreading them evenly through the water. It's still there; you could taste it, and if you boiled the water away the salt would be left behind.
column29: Would the water taste any different now?

column9: Which of these is a solution?
column14: Salt completely dissolved in water
column15: Oil and water shaken together
column16: Sand stirred quickly into a cup of water
column17: Pebbles in a bucket of water
column28: In a solution, one substance is dissolved evenly in another, so you can't see separate pieces and nothing settles out. Salt water is a solution. Sand, oil, and pebbles don't dissolve in water; they just mix or settle, so they aren't solutions.
column29: In a solution, the dissolved substance can't be seen and doesn't settle to the bottom.

column9: Match each everyday observation to the property of water it shows.
column14: Splashing water on your face on a hot day cools you as it dries :: Evaporative cooling
column15: A birdbath freezes on top while the water below stays liquid :: Ice is less dense than liquid water
column16: Raindrops cling to the underside of a car's side mirror :: Adhesion
column17: Drink-mix powder disappears when stirred into water :: Water dissolves many substances
column28: Drying water takes heat with it (evaporative cooling). Ice forming on top shows ice is less dense. Water hanging on to a mirror is water sticking to a different substance (adhesion). Powder disappearing is water acting as a solvent.
column29: For each one, ask: is water changing temperature, changing state, sticking, or dissolving?

column9: Water molecules are polar. Put these steps in order to explain how that lets a small insect stand on a pond.
column14: Molecules at the surface are pulled sideways and downward by their neighbors, but not upward by the air.
column15: A light insect can stand on the surface without sinking.
column16: Neighboring water molecules attract each other with hydrogen bonds.
column17: The surface acts like a stretched, elastic skin.
column28: Polar molecules attract their neighbors through hydrogen bonds. At the surface, there are no water molecules above to pull back, so the surface molecules are pulled sideways and down and hold together tightly. That makes the surface act like a stretched skin, which can hold up a light insect.
column29: Start with the attraction between molecules and end with the insect.

column9: Which property of water most directly lets the chemical reactions inside a cell happen?
column14: Ice floats on liquid water
column15: Water dissolves many substances, so molecules can move through the cytoplasm and meet
column16: Water is clear
column17: Water's surface tension, which holds the cell's molecules close together so they can react
column28: For two molecules to react, they have to move around and bump into each other. Water dissolves sugars, salts, and many other molecules, so they can move freely through the cytoplasm and meet. Floating ice and surface tension matter for life, but not for reactions inside the cell.
column29: For two molecules to react, they have to be able to move and bump into each other.

column9: A space probe finds a lake of liquid on a cold moon. The liquid's molecules are nonpolar and cannot form hydrogen bonds. Compared with water, which predictions are reasonable? Choose all that apply.
column14: It would have weaker surface tension
column15: It would have a higher specific heat than water
column16: It would climb higher than water in thin glass tubes
column17: It would dissolve table salt poorly
column18: Its solid form would most likely sink in its liquid form
column28: Without charged ends, the liquid can't pull ions apart, so salt won't dissolve well. Floating ice comes from hydrogen bonds holding molecules in an open pattern; without them, the solid would be denser than the liquid and sink, like most substances. Weaker attractions also mean weaker surface tension, a lower specific heat, and less climbing up glass.
column29: For each choice, ask: does water's version of this depend on polarity or hydrogen bonds?

column9: Which of these are true properties of water? Choose all that apply.
column14: It takes a lot of heat energy to evaporate
column15: It is a nonpolar molecule
column16: Its solid form sinks in its liquid form
column17: It has a high specific heat
column28: Water has a high specific heat, dissolves many substances, and needs a lot of energy to evaporate, all because it is polar and forms hydrogen bonds. Water is polar, not nonpolar, and its solid form (ice) floats.
column29: Water is polar and forms hydrogen bonds. Check each choice against that.

column9: Water's cohesion is caused by ___ bonds that form between neighboring water molecules.
column28: Hydrogen bonds between a slightly positive hydrogen on one molecule and the slightly negative oxygen on another make water molecules stick together. The common mistake is answering covalent; covalent bonds hold atoms together inside one molecule, not between molecules.
column29: These bonds are named after the atom that is slightly positive.
